data.text/markdown:
8. Your dbt project

Say your analytics team runs dbt build every hour, and the project has grown to hundreds of tests. Each one is a query against the warehouse, on every build, and most of them have never failed. A few of them will fail the day an upstream table changes, and the dashboard will show the gap before anyone reads the log. We'll write a small dbt project, compile it, and have sverify-dbt prove which tests hold on every run before the models run. Then we'll read what it can't prove, fix the model, and list the tests dbt build can skip.

1. A project with tests

The project reads a source table, orders, and its tests say what we know of the data: the keys are never NULL, the order id is unique, a status is one of three. A model, orders_by_customer, totals each customer's orders, and tests its own result:

The model's tests, models/orders_by_customer.yml: 
version: 2
    models:

        - name: orders_by_customer
        columns:

        - name: customer_id
            data_tests: [not_null, unique]

        - name: orders
            data_tests: [not_null]

        - name: revenue
            data_tests: [not_null]
The source's, models/sources.yml, say what we know of orders. Its columns carry data_types, which sverify-dbt reads where dbt docs generate has written no catalogue.

2. Check it before the models run

dbt compile writes each model's SQL. sverify_dbt.check(project) reads it, and proves each model's SQL against the tests on what it reads:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
orders_by_customer (models/orders_by_customer.sql)
  proved before the model runs (dbt build may skip them):
    not_null(customer_id)
    unique(customer_id)
    not_null(orders)
  not proved (dbt build still runs them):
    not_null(revenue): sverify cannot rule out a row that fails it, from the tests upstream
      counterexample: orders(order_id, customer_id, status, amount) = [(0, 0, 'placed', None)] gives (customer_id, orders, revenue) = [(0, 1, None)]
      would hold with, on source('app', 'orders'), column amount: not_null
  assumes sum(amount) does not overflow (DuckDB raises if it does)

1 model(s), 0 refused; 4 test(s): 3 proved, 1 not proved, 0 not checked

data.text/markdown:
Three of the model's tests are proved. customer_id is the grouping key, so unique holds whatever the data is, and not_null follows from the source's test. orders is a count, never NULL. A proved test holds on every run whose inputs pass their tests, so dbt build may leave it out. not_null(revenue) is not proved, and the report says why with a counterexample: a customer whose only order has no amount. A SUM of NULLs is NULL, and the source never promised an amount.

3. Fix the model, and prove it again

We have two ways out: a not_null test on the source's amount, or a model that never returns NULL. We take the second:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
orders_by_customer (models/orders_by_customer.sql)
  proved before the model runs (dbt build may skip them):
    not_null(customer_id)
    unique(customer_id)
    not_null(orders)
    not_null(revenue)
  assumes sum(amount) does not overflow (DuckDB raises if it does)

1 model(s), 0 refused; 4 test(s): 4 proved, 0 not proved, 0 not checked

data.text/markdown:
All four tests hold on every run now. The report keeps one line of caution: sum(amount) can overflow a 64-bit integer, and DuckDB raises where it does, so a run needs amounts that stay small.

4. Leave the proved tests out of the build

write_selectors adds a dbt selector, sverify_proved, to the project's selectors.yml. The command line does the same with sverify-dbt check . --selectors:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
selectors:
- name: sverify_proved
  description: Tests sverify-dbt proved from the tests upstream; generated, do not
    edit
  definition:
    union:
    - method: fqn
      value: not_null_orders_by_customer_customer_id
    - method: fqn
      value: not_null_orders_by_customer_orders
    - method: fqn
      value: not_null_orders_by_customer_revenue
    - method: fqn
      value: unique_orders_by_customer_customer_id

data.text/markdown:
dbt build --exclude selector:sverify_proved runs the models and the tests sverify-dbt couldn't prove. The tests it left out can't fail while the tests upstream pass, because dbt build skips the models downstream of a failing test.

5. What it refuses

Sverify-dbt refuses a model it can't read, with the reason and what to do. We add two: one reads a table by its name, and one is a recursive query:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
chain (models/chain.sql)
  refused: sverify cannot read WITH RECURSIVE yet (#320)

stale_orders (models/stale_orders.sql)
  refused: it reads raw_orders, which is no ref or source of the model (a hard-coded table name, or one a macro wrote); read it with {{ ref() }} or {{ source() }}

2 model(s), 2 refused; 0 test(s): 0 proved, 0 not proved, 0 not checked

data.text/markdown: The first refusal names its exit: read the table with {{ ref() }} or {{ source() }}, so that sverify-dbt knows which tests describe it. The second names the construct, WITH RECURSIVE, and the issue that tracks it. A refused model proves nothing, so dbt build still runs every test on it, and the project's other models are checked as before. You can now prove a dbt project's tests before its models run, read what it couldn't prove and why, fix a model until it holds, and let dbt build skip the tests that can't fail. That is the end of the tour. The sverify-dbt README lists the tests it reads, and the guide covers every feature in more detail.
